title: The High Priestess Tarot Meaning: Upright & Reversed
description: The High Priestess upright: intuition, inner knowing; reversed: outside noise. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Ask your question.
h1: The High Priestess Tarot Card Meaning
image_alt: The High Priestess, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a woman in a pale blue mantle sits between a black pillar marked B and a white one marked J, a scroll in her lap and a yellow crescent at her feet.
capsule: The High Priestess, card II of the Major Arcana, means intuition, inner knowing and stillness: what you understand once you stop pushing. Reversed, outside noise drowns that quiet voice, or secrets and withdrawal take over. A calm, wise card, it asks you not to force answers. Her scroll stays partly covered, and so does her yes-or-no answer: not clear yet.

blocks.heading: What is on The High Priestess card?
paragraphs: A woman in a pale blue mantle sits between two pillars, one black and one white, with a curtain hung behind her. Waite seats her "between the white and black pillars—J. and B.—of the mystic Temple" and adds that "the veil of the Temple is behind her: it is embroidered with palms and pomegranates" (p. 76). On the 1909 card the pillars are the largest shapes: the black one on the left carries a white B, the pale one on the right a dark J, and the pomegranates show red seeds.

She wears "a horned diadem on her head, with a globe in the middle place, and a large solar cross on her breast", with "the lunar crescent" at her feet (p. 76). On the 1909 card the crescent is yellow and her robe spills over it like water, the cross is white, and II sits above her crown.

In her lap lies a scroll. Waite says it bears the word Tora and "is partly covered by her mantle, to shew that some things are implied and some spoken" (p. 76). On the 1909 card the letters TORA can be read on the roll, part of which stays under the blue cloth.
Her clothes, in Waite's words, are "flowing and gauzy, and the mantle suggests light—a shimmering radiance" (p. 76).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The High Priestess?
paragraphs: The upright words circle around what is hidden or not yet shown, and then around the qualities that keep it: silence, tenacity, wisdom, learning. The reversed words swap that quiet depth for heat and display: passion, ardour, conceit, and knowledge that stays on the surface.

Waite held this card in high regard. He wrote that "there are some respects in which this card is the highest and holiest of the Greater Arcana" (p. 79) and called her "the Secret Tradition and the higher sense of the instituted Mysteries" (p. 13).

blocks.heading: What does The High Priestess mean upright?
paragraphs: Intuition comes first with The High Priestess upright: knowing something before you can explain it. A hunch, a dream that stays with you through the day, a feeling that keeps coming back are her territory. The card tends to appear when more effort or more information will not bring the answer you need.
Her gift is stillness. She does not move or argue; she listens. That is not passivity but attention, the kind that notices what is said and what is only implied, and gives both their weight.

Mystery belongs to the meaning, too, along with what modern readings call the subconscious: knowledge that sits below the surface until you are quiet enough to hear it. Not every question is ready to be answered, and the card lets you keep one open a little longer instead of closing it too early. Where this matches your life, ask what part of it you already sense but cannot yet explain.

blocks.heading: What does The High Priestess mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The High Priestess often points to ignored intuition: an inner voice drowned out by outside noise, by advice from every side or by a schedule with no quiet in it. It can also show secrets and unspoken things, something you sense and have not named, even to yourself, and withdrawal: shutting yourself off, going silent instead of saying what is wrong.

Waite's reversed list goes another way, toward passion, conceit and surface knowledge, the loud opposite of her calm. That last phrase is worth keeping: are you skimming a situation instead of letting it sink in? The drowned-out voice is a modern reading, not Waite's.
The remedy is simple, if not always easy: step back from outside opinions for a while and notice what remains underneath them.

blocks.heading: What does The High Priestess mean in love?
paragraphs: Trusting what you sense before looking for answers outside yourself is where The High Priestess starts in matters of the heart. Some feelings need quiet time before they become clear, and the card gives you permission not to name them yet.

Without a partner, the card may ask you to keep your own pace rather than hurry toward someone because it seems expected. With a partner, it may mean paying attention to what you feel in calm moments, not only in loud ones, and keeping an inner space that belongs to you.
Secrets, distance and silence mark the reversed card in love: feelings kept hidden, a hunch brushed aside, something that weighs on you and stays unsaid. Is any of that yours to name?

blocks.heading: What does The High Priestess mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Observation before action is the working style The High Priestess favors. Watch, listen, take note of what goes unsaid in meetings, and let your judgment settle before you commit. Research, study and quiet expertise belong here as well.

In money matters the card stands for what is not fully visible yet: information still to come, finances kept private, a choice made on instinct as well as on numbers. Reversed, the money meaning is hidden or half-read information: a detail left out, or noise around you that covers what matters.

blocks.heading: What is The High Priestess's advice?
paragraphs: Sleep on your question, and when you wake, notice the first feeling that comes, before you check your phone or ask anyone. Let your own knowing speak first; other voices can come after.

blocks.heading: Is The High Priestess a yes or no card?
The High Priestess as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Reserved, observant and hard to read: The High Priestess in human form is the quiet one who notices everything and says little, and she can also be the part of you that understands more than it shows. In the language of feelings, the card means deep interest kept under the surface: attraction felt more than said, a strong intuitive bond, emotions held back until the moment feels right. Reversed, those feelings stay hidden: withdrawal, emotional distance, secrets, a coolness that may cover something unspoken, or signals that are hard to read.

blocks.heading: The High Priestess with other cards

pairs.text: Intuition in a foggy landscape. Trust your inner sense, but give unclear things time to show their shape.
A stalled choice. Stop weighing the options aloud and ask what you already sense.
A double call for quiet. Time alone may show you more than any advice.
Intuition and empathy together. Listen to your own feelings with the care you usually give to others.

blocks.heading: The High Priestess or The Hierophant?
paragraphs: Both figures sit between two pillars, yet Waite insists that the pillars of The Hierophant belong to a different place from the Temple she keeps (p. 88). He raises his right hand in a sign; she, Waite points out, makes none (p. 88). Today the Hierophant is read as tradition, learning and guidance that comes from outside. The High Priestess is knowledge from within: silent, personal, not handed down.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The High Priestess
paragraphs: What do I already know about this that nobody told me?
Which hunch have I been talking myself out of?
Where could I make room for a little silence in my day?

faq.q: Is The High Priestess a good or bad card?
faq.a: Good, though its help is quiet. Because it does not push for results, it can feel frustrating when you want a quick answer, yet what it supports is worth the wait: intuition, patience and listening before you act. Just don't force a decision that your inner sense has not caught up with.

faq.q: Does The High Priestess mean someone is keeping a secret?
faq.a: It can: secrets belong to this card. Waite's list does open with "secrets, mystery" (p. 283), and modern readings use it for hidden information or something not yet said, on any side of a situation. That is the card's meaning, not a verdict on what a particular person hides. The useful question is what is still unsaid, including by you.

faq.q: Does The High Priestess represent a woman?
faq.a: In Waite's day it could. His list says the card may stand for "the Querent herself, if female" (p. 283), and his forty-two-card method uses it to mark a woman who asks (p. 308). Today it describes a quality anyone can have: observant, unhurried, guided from within.

faq.q: What other names does The High Priestess have?
faq.a: Older decks called her "the Pope Joan, or Female Pontiff", Waite writes, and some early writers named her "the Mother, or Pope's Wife", which he found "opposed to the symbolism" (p. 13). In the 1909 deck the title printed at the bottom of the card is The High Priestess.

waite.quote: Secrets, mystery, the future as yet unrevealed … silence, tenacity; mystery, wisdom, science. Reversed: Passion, moral or physical ardour, conceit, surface knowledge.
